strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: preserving useful accumulated knowledge during context adaptation. Structured delta updates and separate reflection and curation roles form a clear, plausible engineering approach.

Reports substantial improvements across agent and financial tasks. Offline AppWorld performance rises from 42.4 to 59.4, versus 46.4 for GEPA; supervised offline Formula accuracy improves from 67.5 to 85.5.

Includes relevant prompt-optimization and adaptive-memory baselines, component ablations, adaptation-cost measurements, and extensive prompt examples. Using the same model across ACE roles avoids confounding gains with a stronger teacher.
Acknowledges feedback-dependent failures, including degraded FiNER performance without supervision, rather than presenting adaptation as universally beneficial.
weaknesses: The central methodological contribution is insufficiently isolated. Table 3 ablates reflection and additional epochs, but not delta updates, deduplication, or helpful/harmful counters. There is no simple append-only memory baseline or length-controlled comparison. Consequently, the results do not establish whether ACE's proposed mechanisms outperform straightforward accumulation or whether longer contexts explain the gains.

The online AppWorld comparison is confounded by initialization. Table 3 reveals that the headline 59.5 result includes offline warmup; ACE without warmup scores 56.1, versus 51.9 for DC. Equivalent warmup for DC is not reported, and Table 1 does not identify this distinction. Comparisons between online adaptation and leaderboard agents also require explicit alignment of permitted cross-task learning and feedback.

The claim of learning from natural execution feedback alone needs a precise feedback specification. The AppWorld Reflector prompt includes reference code and task unit-test reports, but the manuscript does not clearly document which fields are removed in each no-ground-truth condition. Benchmark success tests can provide privileged supervision beyond ordinary execution errors; the current description does not resolve this distinction.

Experimental reliability and reproducibility are inadequate. Dataset sample counts, financial-task preprocessing and answer construction, sampling settings, actual adaptation stopping criteria, and validation-based context selection are insufficiently documented. Results lack repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and sensitivity to test ordering, despite the path dependence of online memory. Evaluation uses only one backbone.

Claims about preventing context collapse and scalable refinement exceed the evidence. Figure 2 presents a single collapse trajectory without repeated controlled comparisons. The deduplication embedding model, threshold, pruning policy, and context budget are unspecified; appendix Curator prompts expose only ADD operations, leaving correction and removal behavior unclear. Long-horizon robustness and bounded memory growth are not demonstrated.

Efficiency evidence covers only two selected comparisons and lacks sufficient accounting for hardware, concurrency, caching, and full serving costs. The 86.9% headline averages reductions from different tasks and baselines. Adaptation savings are promising, but do not establish that increasingly long playbooks have low end-to-end overhead.

Novelty relative to existing agent-memory systems remains mostly architectural and empirical. A-MEM and Agent Workflow Memory are discussed but not evaluated, and the broader-context framing alone does not establish a substantive advance over structured memory accumulation. Together with the unresolved evaluation issues, this leaves the paper below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: Addresses a practical problem: preserving useful accumulated knowledge during iterative context adaptation. Structured incremental updates are a sensible, interpretable engineering solution.
Reports substantial improvements against relevant baselines. Offline ACE achieves 59.4 average on AppWorld versus GEPA’s 46.4, and 81.9 average on the financial benchmarks versus GEPA’s 72.5.
Uses the same backbone across ACE roles, includes supervised and unsupervised adaptation settings, provides prompts, and acknowledges degradation when reliable feedback is unavailable.
weaknesses: The contribution is insufficiently isolated from existing memory approaches. ACE explicitly builds on Dynamic Cheatsheet, while structured memory and reflection are established ideas. Table 3 ablates reflection, multiple epochs, and warmup, but not the central delta-update or grow-and-refine mechanisms. Comparisons against simple append-only memory, length-controlled rewriting, and related structured-memory methods are needed to establish what is responsible for the gains.

The main online AppWorld comparison confounds adaptation with initialization. Table 3 reveals that the 59.5 result reported in Table 1 includes offline warmup; ACE without warmup scores 56.1. Equivalent warmup for Dynamic Cheatsheet is not reported. ACE still improves over DC’s 51.9, but the headline 7.6-point advantage cannot be attributed solely to the online method.

Feedback access is not specified precisely enough to substantiate the label-free claim. The AppWorld Reflector prompt includes reference code and unit-test reports, whereas the narrative emphasizes natural execution feedback. The paper should explicitly state which fields and evaluator signals remain available in every no-ground-truth condition. This is an unresolved protocol ambiguity, not evidence of demonstrated leakage.

Evaluation and reproducibility details are incomplete. Dataset counts, financial-task preprocessing and answer construction, decoding settings, validation-based context selection, and repeated-run uncertainty are not reported. Online results use a single shared shuffled order without assessing order sensitivity. Testing only DeepSeek-V3.1 also limits support for broad claims about language models.

The grow-and-refine mechanism is underspecified: the embedding model, similarity threshold, pruning policy, context budget, and refinement schedule are missing. Published Curator prompts expose only ADD operations, leaving the implementation of correction and removal unclear. The single context-collapse example does not establish failure frequency or demonstrate sustained prevention across runs.

Efficiency evidence covers only two selected method–task comparisons and adaptation costs. It does not establish end-to-end serving efficiency, including longer-context inference, cache behavior, or warmup. The discussion of caching is plausible but unmeasured; averaging the two latency reductions into a general 86.9% headline overstates the scope of the evidence.

Several claims exceed the results: label-free online FiNER falls from 70.7 to 67.3, ACE trails DC on AppWorld test-normal SGC, and the leaderboard comparison mixes online adaptation with systems whose adaptation protocols are not established as equivalent. The claimed smaller model relative to GPT-4.1 is also unsupported by disclosed model sizes.

strengths: ACE addresses a practical problem: preserving useful accumulated knowledge during repeated context updates. Structured delta updates and separate reflection and curation roles form a clear, plausible engineering approach.

The reported offline gains are substantial: AppWorld average performance improves from 46.4 with GEPA to 59.4 with ACE, while Formula accuracy improves from 71.5 to 85.5. These results suggest useful benefits beyond standard prompt optimization.

The evaluation includes agent tasks and financial applications, established baselines, and both offline and online adaptation. Using the same model for ACE's three roles avoids confounding improvements with a stronger teacher model.
The paper provides component prompts, some ablations, and adaptation-cost measurements. It also candidly reports degradation without reliable feedback, including the decline on FiNER.
weaknesses: The headline online comparison is confounded by initialization. Table 3 identifies the 59.5 AppWorld result reported in Table 1 as ACE with offline warmup; ACE without warmup achieves 56.1. An equivalent warmup is not documented for Dynamic Cheatsheet. The remaining improvement over DC's 51.9 is promising, but the claimed 7.6-point advantage does not isolate the online adaptation method.

The label-free feedback protocol is insufficiently specified. The AppWorld Reflector prompt includes ground-truth code and unit-test reports, whereas the main text describes natural execution feedback. The paper should explicitly identify which fields are removed and whether benchmark evaluator outputs remain available in each condition. This distinction is essential to assessing the central claim of self-improvement without labeled supervision and the comparability of leaderboard results.

The experiments do not isolate the principal methodological contributions. Table 3 ablates reflection and additional training epochs, but not delta updates, semantic deduplication, or helpful/harmful counters. There is no controlled comparison with DC augmented only by incremental updates, nor a context-length-matched comparison. The single context-collapse example does not establish how frequently the problem occurs or whether simpler safeguards suffice.

Reproducibility and statistical evidence are inadequate. Dataset sample counts and financial-task preprocessing, decoding settings, stopping and checkpoint-selection rules, context budgets, and deduplication configurations are not sufficiently documented. Results lack repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and sensitivity to online example ordering. Only one backbone is evaluated, limiting support for broad claims about language models.

The novelty over existing agent-memory systems is modest and incompletely established. ACE explicitly builds on Dynamic Cheatsheet, while reflection and structured evolving memories already appear in cited work. Relevant systems such as A-MEM and Agent Workflow Memory are discussed but not experimentally compared; claiming broader applicability does not establish a distinct technical advance.

The efficiency evidence covers selected adaptation workloads rather than end-to-end deployment. Table 4 does not establish comparable accuracy–cost tradeoffs across budgets or account clearly for warmup and the recurring inference cost of longer playbooks. The discussion of caching is plausible but unmeasured. Overall, the promising gains do not yet overcome the unresolved comparison, protocol, and reproducibility issues required for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: ACE addresses a practically important problem: retaining useful experience during repeated context adaptation. Structured playbooks, localized updates, and separate reflection and curation provide a clear, implementable approach.

The reported improvements are substantial. Offline AppWorld performance rises from 46.4 with GEPA to 59.4 with ACE; supervised financial-task accuracy averages 81.9 versus GEPA’s 72.5. These gains warrant serious consideration.

The appendix strengthens the empirical contribution with additional model families, medical reasoning, and text-to-SQL. Ablations support incremental updates, reflection, and multi-epoch adaptation; removing incremental updates reduces AppWorld test-normal average performance from 70.3 to 56.9.

The paper examines feedback quality, harmful reflections, hyperparameter sensitivity, and component-level token costs, and acknowledges that adaptation can degrade performance when reliable feedback is unavailable.
weaknesses: The headline online comparison is not cleanly controlled. Table 3 reveals that the 59.5 AppWorld result reported as online ACE in Table 1 includes offline warmup; ACE without warmup scores 56.1. Equivalent initialization is not established for Dynamic Cheatsheet. Both methods should be compared with matched training access and warmup budgets.

Efficiency claims need reconciliation. Table 4 reports 357 ACE rollouts versus 1,434 for GEPA, whereas Table 12 reports 2,075 versus 1,455. Different settings or counting conventions may explain this, but they are not reconciled. Moreover, the detailed cost study uses one epoch and one reflection round instead of the main configuration’s maxima of five, without reporting corresponding accuracy. Evaluation input tokens increase by 117.4%, and ACE’s cache discount alone does not establish lower serving cost than an equally cached baseline.

Statistical reliability is insufficiently established: results lack repeated runs, confidence intervals, and sensitivity to shuffled online task order. Exact dataset sizes and preprocessing for the main financial experiments are also insufficiently specified. This matters especially for smaller differences and claims of robust hyperparameter behavior.

The methodological novelty is primarily a combination of existing reflection and structured-memory ideas. Comparisons against A-MEM, Agent Workflow Memory, and simple append-only or retrieval-based memory would better establish the contribution beyond Dynamic Cheatsheet. The incremental-update ablation is useful, but does not isolate the benefit of the full framework over these simpler alternatives.

Important protocol and implementation details remain ambiguous. The AppWorld Reflector prompt includes reference code and task unit-test reports, but the paper does not precisely specify which fields remain available in the no-ground-truth setting. The embedding model, default deduplication settings, pruning rules, and reflection stopping procedure also need clearer specification for reproducibility.

Some claims exceed the evidence. BIRD-SQL is evaluated with an LLM judge rather than execution accuracy, and ACE’s overall advantage over GEPA is only 0.7 points. The leaderboard comparison mixes adaptation regimes, calls 59.4 a match to 60.3 without uncertainty estimates, and describes DeepSeek-V3.1 as smaller than GPT-4.1 without establishing GPT-4.1’s size. Overall, the promising gains are not yet supported by sufficiently controlled and reproducible evidence for a clear acceptance.

strengths: ACE addresses a practical failure mode of adaptive agent memory with a clear, implementable design: structured playbooks, incremental updates, and separate reflection and curation.
The main performance gains are substantial. Offline AppWorld performance rises from 46.4 with GEPA to 59.4 with ACE; supervised offline finance accuracy averages 81.9 versus GEPA’s 72.5.
The appendix meaningfully broadens the evidence through additional model families, medical reasoning, and text-to-SQL experiments. The benefits are not confined to a single backbone or finance task.

Ablations support the proposed mechanism. Removing incremental updates substantially reduces AppWorld performance, while separate experiments examine reflection, multiple epochs, warmup, feedback corruption, and context limits.
The paper acknowledges important failures, including degradation on FiNER without reliable feedback, and provides extensive prompts and component-level token accounting.
weaknesses: Novelty is primarily an engineering synthesis of reflection, external memory, and incremental editing. Comparisons against A-MEM, Agent Workflow Memory, or a simple append-and-deduplicate memory baseline would better establish the contribution beyond existing memory systems.

The headline online comparison is partly confounded by initialization: Table 3 reveals that the 59.5 AppWorld result includes offline warmup, whereas ACE without warmup achieves 56.1. DC is not shown with equivalent warmup. The remaining improvement is encouraging, but the headline difference cannot be attributed solely to online adaptation.

Efficiency claims require reconciliation. Table 4 reports 75.1% fewer rollouts, while Table 12 reports 42.6% more. Different configurations or counting conventions may explain this, but these are not adequately reconciled. Moreover, the detailed cost study uses one epoch and one reflection round rather than the main configuration, without reporting corresponding accuracy.

Serving-cost evidence is incomplete. ACE consumes 117.4% more evaluation input tokens than GEPA in Table 14. The caching experiment measures savings relative to ACE’s own uncached cost, without an equivalent cached GEPA comparison or an end-to-end cost comparison at matched accuracy.

Statistical reliability and reproducibility remain limited: no repeated-run uncertainty or sensitivity to test-stream ordering is reported, and exact dataset subsets, decoding settings, and deduplication/pruning implementation details are incompletely specified. The no-label AppWorld protocol also needs an explicit account of which feedback fields are available, since the supplied Reflector prompt includes reference code and unit-test reports.

Some generalization claims exceed the evidence. BIRD-SQL uses an unvalidated GPT-4o-mini judge rather than execution accuracy, and ACE’s overall advantage over GEPA is only 0.7 points, with worse results on harder subsets. Claims of universally consistent superiority and broadly low overhead should be narrowed.

strengths: ACE addresses a practical problem with a clear design: structured playbooks, localized updates, and separate reflection and curation preserve accumulated knowledge without repeatedly rewriting the entire context.
The main performance improvements are substantial. Offline ACE reaches 59.4 versus GEPA’s 46.4 on AppWorld’s aggregate metric, and 81.9 versus 72.5 on the finance average.

Evaluation extends beyond the primary backbone and finance tasks. Results across additional model families and medical reasoning provide meaningful evidence of generality, although text-to-SQL gains are modest.

Ablations support the proposed mechanisms: removing incremental updates substantially reduces AppWorld performance, while reflection and multiple adaptation epochs provide further gains. Additional feedback-corruption and hyperparameter experiments strengthen the empirical analysis.
The paper explicitly reports failures without reliable feedback, including degraded online FiNER performance, providing a useful qualification of its self-improvement claims.
weaknesses: Efficiency claims are not consistently supported by matched configurations. Appendix A.3 measures ACE with one epoch and one reflection round, unlike the stronger main configuration. Table 4 reports 75.1% fewer rollouts, whereas Table 12 reports 42.6% more; differing configurations or rollout definitions need reconciliation. Evaluation input tokens also increase by 117.4%, and the caching study does not establish comparative serving costs under identical caching conditions.

The headline online AppWorld result includes offline warmup, as Table 3 reveals, while equivalent warmup for Dynamic Cheatsheet is not established. ACE still improves without warmup, but the headline comparison conflates initialization and online adaptation benefits.

Results lack repeated runs, confidence intervals, and sensitivity to test-stream ordering. This particularly limits conclusions about smaller cross-model gains, hyperparameter robustness, and the 0.7-point advantage over GEPA on BIRD-SQL.

BIRD-SQL is evaluated by GPT-4o-mini judgment rather than execution accuracy, without demonstrating agreement with executable correctness. This weakens the evidence for improved structured code generation.

Novelty is primarily a useful combination of existing reflection and memory mechanisms. Comparisons against structured agent-memory approaches, or a simple append-only reflection baseline with matched context and compute budgets, would better establish the value of the full architecture.

Reproduction and interpretation require clearer implementation details, including embedding-based deduplication, pruning rules, stopping criteria, and the exact feedback available in no-ground-truth experiments. The supplied AppWorld Reflector prompt includes unit-test reports and reference-code fields, but their treatment in these experiments is insufficiently specified.
